title: Office Application Startup: Outlook Home Page
shortTitle: Office Application Startup: Outlook Home Page
summary: The Outlook Home Page is a legacy folder property that replaces the normal list view of a mailbox folder with a web page, which Outlook renders using its embedded browser engine. The property accepts a local path or a remote address, and the page is fetched and displayed whenever that folder is opened or refreshed and again when Outlook starts with the folder in view. Abuse is therefore a two part operation: set the Home Page property of a folder such as the Inbox to attacker controlled content, then wait for the page to load, at which point scripting inside the page executes in the context of the Outlook process. Because the payload is a web page rather than a macro or an executable, it leaves almost nothing on the file system, and the only durable trace is the folder property itself plus the outbound request used to retrieve the content. On current builds the feature is disabled by default and is governed by an administrator policy, so its appearance in a modern environment is itself a strong signal. Distinguishing malicious use from a legitimate one is straightforward in practice, because almost no organisation still deploys Home Page customisations; the defender's main task is knowing where the property is stored and monitoring for changes to it.

beginner.definition: Outlook folders, such as your Inbox, can show a web page instead of the normal list of messages. That setting is called a Home Page. This technique is when an attacker points that setting at a page they control.
beginner.whyItMatters: The attacker writes no file on your computer, so there is little for a scanner to find. The page can run code as soon as you open the folder. Many companies do not use this old feature at all, so any use of it deserves a close look.
howItWorks: Each Outlook folder can be told to display a web address instead of the message list.
The attacker sets that property on a folder you use every day, such as the Inbox.
Outlook remembers the setting in the mailbox, so it stays after you restart Outlook.
When you open or refresh that folder, Outlook fetches and shows the page.
The page contains script, and that script runs with the rights of the Outlook program.
The script can contact the attacker or run other code on your machine.
beginner.example: Think of a noticeboard in a shared flat. One day someone replaces the pin board cover with a poster they printed. Every time a housemate walks past and looks at the board, the ink on the poster gives off a smell that unlocks the front door. The poster is just paper, and nobody thinks to check the board.
takeaways: The trigger is simply opening or refreshing the folder, so no click on a file is needed.
The setting is stored in the mailbox and survives a new computer.
Treat any Home Page setting in a modern organisation as highly unusual.

objectives: Explain what the Outlook Home Page folder property does and where it is stored.
Describe how this sub-technique differs from the parent technique Office Application Startup.
Describe the sequence of events between setting the property and code execution.
Identify the mailbox setting and the network request that reveal this abuse.
Explain why administrators may disable the feature and how that reduces risk.
